chunks: "Both are parts of RAM your program uses for data that isn't fixed at compile time, but they work very differently. The stack is for function calls.
Each call gets a frame holding its locals and return address.
Allocating it is almost free, because the compiler just subtracts from the stack pointer, and it frees itself when the function returns. It's LIFO, fast, and cache friendly.
The downsides are that it's small and fixed in size, and anything on it dies when the function returns, so I can't hand back a pointer to a local.
The heap is for data that has to outlive the function or whose size isn't known until runtime.
I request a block with malloc or new and I have to free it, or a garbage collector does.

It's much more flexible, since blocks can be any size and live any length of time, but it's slower because the allocator has to search for free space, and it brings leaks, fragmentation and the possibility that an allocation just fails.
In embedded systems I lean on the stack and static allocation, and I'm cautious with the heap.
A device that runs for years can fragment its heap and hit an allocation failure in the field that you never saw in testing.
If I need dynamic-like behavior I'll use fixed-size pools."
